notes.meaning: Solomon spent twenty years carrying out his two greatest building projects. It took seven years to finish the temple of the Lord and thirteen years to build the royal palace. These years marked a time of peace, stability, and great blessing for Israel.

King Hiram of Tyre had returned these northern towns to Solomon because they did not suit his needs. Solomon repaired the damaged towns and settled Israelites in them. This expanded Israel's secure living area and protected the northern border.

Solomon marched his army to the region of Hamath-zobah and captured it. King David had made this area pay tribute years earlier, but its people seem to have rebelled. Solomon acted firmly to restore peace and secure the kingdom's borders.

Solomon fortified Tadmor, an oasis city in the desert later called Palmyra, and built supply towns in Hamath. These store cities held food, weapons, and treasures along major trade routes. They kept the army supplied and protected travelers from raiders.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early commentators like Calmet and Haydock identify Tadmor with the later city of Emesa on the Orontes River.

notes.meaning: Solomon strengthened Upper and Lower Beth-horon by adding strong stone walls, heavy gates, and iron bars. These two towns sat on a steep mountain pass that led straight toward Jerusalem. Making them strong forts guarded the central heartland of Israel against foreign armies.

Solomon continued to build storage towns, fortress cities, and military bases for his chariot teams and horses across the land. God gave him success in all his plans, allowing him to complete everything he set his heart to build. Solomon also showed wisdom by knowing when his building goals were met so he could stop.

differ.view: Building chariot cities went against God's law in Deuteronomy forbidding kings to multiply horses, hinting that Solomon was starting to trust in military power rather than in God alone.

notes.meaning: Descendants of the original Canaanite tribes still lived in the land because Israel had never driven them out completely. Solomon drafted these non-Israelites into forced labor gangs for his vast building projects. They carried the heavy physical burden of cutting stone and hauling materials.

Solomon protected the people of Israel from being treated as slave laborers. Instead, Israelites served in honorable roles as soldiers, commanders, and chariot leaders. Their duty was to defend the land and lead the nation under the king.

Solomon placed two hundred and fifty chief officers in charge of the nationwide building work. These men were Israelite leaders assigned to supervise the labor crews and keep the projects orderly. Good organization helped the kingdom finish massive tasks efficiently.

Solomon moved his wife, the princess of Egypt, out of the City of David into a palace he built specially for her. He recognized that the place where the holy ark of God had rested was sacred ground and should not be treated as a normal home. Even though he had made an alliance with Egypt, he still showed a real concern for God's holiness.

differ.view: Marrying Pharaoh's daughter was an unwise political move that began Solomon's spiritual decline, and moving her house could not keep the danger of her idols out of the kingdom.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic commentators suggest Pharaoh's daughter may have appeared to accept the true faith at first but later showed signs of returning to pagan ways, making it unfitting for her to stay where the ark had been.

notes.meaning: With the temple fully dedicated, Solomon offered burnt offerings on the bronze altar in the courtyard. A burnt offering was an animal sacrifice completely consumed by fire as a gift of total devotion to the Lord. Worship had now permanently shifted from the old tabernacle at Gibeon to the new temple in Jerusalem.

Solomon followed the law of Moses by maintaining regular sacrifices every morning and evening. He also provided the required offerings for weekly Sabbaths, monthly New Moon celebrations, and the three major annual pilgrim festivals. Keeping this rhythm helped the nation honor God consistently every day of the year.

Solomon organized the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers exactly as his father David had ordered. David was an inspired prophet of God, so Solomon did not change or add to those instructions. Each group knew its daily duty, whether leading musical praise, assisting at the altar, or guarding the temple gates.

The priests and Levites faithfully carried out the royal orders without turning away from a single instruction. They managed the worship services and guarded the temple treasury with honesty and care. Because the king followed God's laws, the religious leaders gladly followed the king's directions.

All the work on the house of the Lord was now complete, from the laying of the foundation stones to the start of daily worship. The building was not considered truly finished until regular prayer and sacrifice were taking place within it. This completed Solomon's greatest assignment for God and Israel.

Solomon traveled south to Ezion-geber and Eloth on the Red Sea coast in the land of Edom. He went in person to inspect these ports so he could set up commercial shipping for his nation. Wise leaders take personal care of important projects to make sure they succeed.

King Hiram sent Phoenician ships and seasoned sailors because Israel had little experience navigating the open seas. The fleet sailed together to the distant port of Ophir and brought back over sixteen tons of gold for Solomon. This showed how nations can work together peacefully, though true treasure is found in God's grace rather than gold.
